rephrase builds a phrase out of fragments, using the grammar of each.

IT IS NOT WHAT ITS NAME SUGGESTS:
It does not simplify a sentence. It ACCUMULATES. Each fragment you send is compared with the phrase built so far, part by part:

- if the phrase already has a part of the same kind - a noun phrase, a
  phrase starting with a preposition, a verb, an adjective - and the two are
  close enough in meaning, the new fragment REPLACES that part
- otherwise the fragment is added on the end, after a comma

Send it these, one at a time:

    a woman          -> a woman
    in a red coat    -> a woman, in a red coat
    she is walking   -> a woman , in a red walking coat
    a tall man       -> a tall man in a red walking coat
    in a blue coat   -> a tall man in a blue coat
    not blue         -> a tall man in a coat
    through the park -> a tall man in a coat, through the park
    no               -> a tall man in a coat

(the spacing around the commas really is uneven - it is stitching fragments together, not writing them out)

Look at the third step. 'she' was taken to mean the woman it has been tracking, and the verb was folded in as a modifier rather than appended - which is how 'a red walking coat' happens. That is the character of this node: it is a generative instrument that produces compressed, slightly strange descriptions, not a grammar engine that produces correct ones. Judge it by whether the results are worth having.

A fragment that starts with 'it', 'they', 'he' or 'she' has that word swapped for the noun the phrase is about. A fragment that starts with 'not' takes a word out: 'not blue' removes the adjective 'blue'.

STEPPING BACK:
'no', 'wrong' and 'go back' return to the previous phrase, whenever they arrive. It remembers only one step: a second 'no' undoes the first, so sending 'no' twice brings back the phrase you stepped away from. Sent before there is any previous phrase, they do nothing.

THE SETTINGS, AND WHICH WAY THEY POINT:
'replace similarity' is how alike in meaning a fragment and a part of the phrase must be before the fragment replaces that part. Raise it and more fragments are added on the end; lower it and more of the phrase gets overwritten. 0.5 by default.

'complexity replace threshold' is an upper limit on what it will try to fold in. Complexity counts nouns, pronouns, verbs and prepositions, plus a quarter of the word count - so 1.5 for 'a woman' and 9 for 'the old man walked slowly across the wide empty square at dawn'. A fragment above the threshold is not folded in: it replaces the whole phrase and the next fragment builds on it. The default of 6 means it works with fragments, not whole sentences. Two exceptions: a fragment whose main word is a preposition is always tried, and a long one that starts with a word like 'and' or 'because' is added on the end.

'clear input pause' is how long a phrase stays live, in seconds. A fragment arriving within that time of the last one is folded into the phrase in progress; after a longer gap, the next fragment starts afresh. 40 by default.

'clip score threshold' goes with the 'clip score' inlet, which is a feedback path. When the score last received there is at or above the threshold the node stops rewriting and sends nothing at all - the reading is that whatever is consuming the phrase is already doing well enough, so leave it alone. A rephrase that has gone quiet is usually this, not a fault. The default of 640 is far above anything the inlet sees until you wire it.

'output as list' sends the result word by word instead of as one string.

SYNTAX:
rephrase

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

text in:
A fragment. Receiving it folds it in and sends the result. A list is joined back into one phrase first, so a message node works as a source.

clip score:
The feedback number. It does not trigger anything; it is held and checked when the next fragment arrives.

MESSAGES:

full_tree <word>:
Sends, as a list, the word and everything that depends on it in the current phrase.

bare_tree <word>:
The same, cut off where the next phrase begins. On 'a tall man in a coat, through the park', 'full_tree man' sends the whole thing and 'bare_tree man' sends 'a tall man'. Only for a noun, verb or
preposition.

Either sends nothing if the word is not in the current phrase.

OUTPUTS:

results:
The accumulated phrase.

THEY ALL SHARE ONE LANGUAGE MODEL:
The first of these nodes to be created loads en_core_web_lg, and every spacy node in every patch then shares it. It is a few hundred megabytes and takes a moment, so the first one costs something and the rest are free.

If the model is not installed the nodes still build, but they do nothing at all - no output, no error each time. A spacy node that is silent when everything is wired correctly is the thing to suspect.

RELATED:
lemma also works from the grammar of a phrase.
spacy_similarity works on meaning rather than grammar. context_tracker keeps track of place, time and actors across a stream of text.
